abstract.t: A COSE Hash Envelope signs the digest of a preimage, not the preimage itself. When the preimage is the encoding of a structured value, such as a CBOR data item, and a verifier holds that value but not the bytes that were hashed, the verifier has to encode the value again, and the digest matches only if it applies the same deterministic encoding as the producer. CBOR permits more than one encoding of the same data item, and the preimage content type does not identify the encoding that was applied. This document defines a COSE Hash Envelope protected-header parameter that identifies the encoding: the integer 1 for the Core Deterministic Encoding Requirements of RFC 8949, or a URL for any other encoding, named by the application profile that uses the parameter. A verifier ignores a value that does not identify an encoding it implements.

note.name: Note to Readers
note.t: Individual submission, intended for the COSE Working Group (cose@ietf.org).
Source for this document, with a reference emitter and verifier and test vectors, is at .

section.name: Introduction
section.t: The COSE Hash Envelope signs the digest of a preimage and identifies the hash algorithm (258), the content type of the preimage (259), and optionally where the preimage can be retrieved (260). A verifier that holds the preimage can check that the digest of it, produced with the hash algorithm identified by payload-hash-alg (258), matches the payload, as Section 5.3 describes. That check needs no information from this document, and retaining the preimage is the simplest way to make it possible.

The Hash Envelope carries the digest, not the preimage, and payload-location (260) is optional. The content therefore reaches a verifier, if at all, from outside the Hash Envelope, in whatever form its application provides, which can be a structured value rather than the bytes that were hashed. The content can arrive as a data item inside a larger CBOR message, and unless the message wraps that item in a byte string, most CBOR decoders cannot return its encoded bytes ( Appendices H.1 and J.1). A system can also store the content in another representation -- for example, a software inventory that keeps Concise Software Identification (CoSWID) tags as records in a database -- rather than keep a second copy of each item as the bytes that were hashed, provided that representation preserves each data item exactly (). To check such content against its Hash Envelope, the verifier has to encode the value again, the case in which Section 5.3.1 says deterministic encoding becomes necessary and notes that designs of this kind are often chosen to reduce data size, preserve privacy, or meet other design constraints. COSE meets the same need for its own Sig_structure, which the signer and the verifier each construct rather than transmit, by fixing how that structure is encoded ( Sections 4.4 and 9). For a Hash Envelope preimage, whose content type the application chooses, COSE fixes no encoding.

Re-encoding reproduces the preimage only if the verifier applies the encoding the producer applied. CBOR permits more than one encoding of the same data item ( Section 4.2), and a producer need not apply a deterministic one: {"x": 1.5} is a1 61 78 f9 3e 00 under the Core Deterministic Encoding Requirements ( Section 4.2.1) and a1 61 78 fb 3f f8 00 00 00 00 00 00 when every floating-point value is written as binary64, and both are valid CBOR. The preimage-content-type (259) names the type of the content, such as application/swid+cbor, not the encoding applied to it. A verifier that assumes an encoding the producer did not state cannot tell a modified value from one encoded another way. The parameter lets the verifier tell the two apart: when the producer states the encoding, a mismatch means the value the verifier holds is not the value the producer encoded. When it does not, nothing changes: the verifier checks the content binding as Section 5.3 describes ().

This document defines one protected-header parameter, deterministic-encodings, which identifies that encoding: the integer 1 identifies the Core Deterministic Encoding Requirements of Section 4.2.1 (), and any other encoding is identified by a URL that an application profile names (). This document defines no encoding of its own. As with the hash algorithm in payload-hash-alg (258), the producer states its choice and the verifier follows it. Naming a canonicalization or a profile by a URI has precedent: XML Signature names the canonicalization algorithm applied to the signed content by a URI ( Section 6.1), and the eat_profile claim names a profile, including the encoding choices it fixes, by a URI or an OID ( Sections 4.3.2 and 6.4). The parameter uses the extension point the Hash Envelope protected header already provides (: * (int / tstr) => any). The encoding is not carried as a media-type parameter of preimage-content-type (259). The application/cbor media type defines no parameters ( Section 9.3), so such a parameter would have to be registered for every media type the encoding applies to, and a CoAP Content-Format number carries only the parameters fixed in its registry entry ( Section 12.3), so each pairing of media type and encoding would also need its own number. A profile that has its own media type, such as application/vnd.ipld.dag-cbor , is already identified by 259; content labelled application/cbor, or with an application's own type such as application/swid+cbor, is not.

The scope of this document is structured values, such as CBOR data items, and the deterministic encodings that serialize them. Media encodings, such as those of images, and builds of software from source code are out of scope; such content is checked from its bytes, as Section 5.3 describes.

section.name: Terminology
section.t: The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here.

"COSE", "COSE_Sign1", and "protected header" are defined in ; "CDDL" in ; "Hash Envelope" and "preimage" in . As in , the payload of a Hash Envelope is a digest, and the preimage consists of the bytes that were hashed to produce it. The Hash Envelope labels this document builds on are 258 (payload-hash-alg), 259 (preimage-content-type), and 260 (payload-location).
This document also uses the following terms:

dd.t: A value with internal structure, such as a CBOR data item, that a deterministic encoding serializes to create a preimage.

A specification of an application or protocol that uses deterministic-encodings and states which encodings its producers apply and its verifiers implement: the one this document identifies by the integer 1, or others, each named by a URL.

The correspondence between content a verifier holds -- a preimage, or a structured value -- and the payload of a Hash Envelope. A verifier checks it as Section 5.3 describes. The check succeeds when the digest of the preimage, held or re-created from a structured value, produced with the hash algorithm identified by payload-hash-alg (258), matches the payload, and the verifier found no inconsistency in the protected header (); otherwise it fails. This document adds no other outcome.

section.name: The deterministic-encodings Header Parameter

dd.t: deterministic-encodings. The deterministic encoding with which a structured value was serialized to create the bytes that were hashed (preimage) to produce the payload, given as the integer 1 or as a URL.

section.t: It extends by adding one optional member to the Hash_Envelope_Protected_Header CDDL of Section 4, alongside the members for labels 258-260. The extended rule restates the rule with that member added:
section.sourcecode: Hash_Envelope_Protected_Header_With_Encoding = { ? &(alg: 1) => int, &(payload_hash_alg: 258) => int, ? &(payload_preimage_content_type: 259) => uint / tstr, ? &(payload_location: 260) => tstr, ? &(deterministic_encodings: TBD_1) => 1 / tstr, * (int / tstr) => any }
section.t: Label TBD_1 MAY be present in the protected header and MUST NOT be present in the unprotected header, following the placement rule states for labels 258 through 260. When label TBD_1 is present, preimage-content-type (259) MUST also be present (). A producer MUST NOT list label TBD_1 in the crit header parameter ( Section 3.1), so that a verifier that implements only can ignore it.

The value of deterministic-encodings is either the unsigned integer 1 or a text string holding a URL. The integer 1 identifies the Core Deterministic Encoding Requirements of Section 4.2.1 (). This document defines no other integer value and creates no registry.

A text string value is a URL: a URI ( Section 3) with the "https" scheme ( Section 4.2.2) that links to the part of a specification that defines exactly one deterministic encoding. When the linked document defines more than one encoding, the URL MUST carry a fragment ( Section 4.2.5) that selects the section defining the encoding that was applied. A producer copies the URL of the encoding it applied. A verifier compares the value with the URLs of the encodings it implements, character by character ( Section 6.2.1), and does not dereference it.

Which URLs a producer can use, and which a verifier acts on, is decided by the application profile that uses this parameter, not by this document; a profile that names a URL is responsible for the URL, the encoding, and the encoding's Applicable Content Types (). No registry of these URLs is needed, and a value that a verifier does not implement changes no verification outcome: the verifier ignores it ().

section.name: The Value for CBOR Content
section.t: For CBOR content, this document defines one value: the integer 1. As the value of deterministic-encodings, 1 states that the structured value was encoded according to the Core Deterministic Encoding Requirements of Section 4.2.1. It does not stand for the other encodings that describes, such as the length-first map key ordering of its Section 4.2.3. For a CBOR sequence , each data item is encoded according to these requirements. The choices that Section 4.2.2 leaves to a protocol, including the representation of NaN values, are not part of this encoding ().

A producer that applied this encoding and includes deterministic-encodings MUST set it to the integer 1, not to a URL, so that producers and verifiers use one value for the encoding. The integer takes 1 byte; the URL of that section on the RFC Editor's site would take 59 bytes.

An RFC does not change once it is published, so the integer 1 names one fixed text. A later specification that changes deterministic encoding is identified by a URL of its own (), and Hash Envelopes that carry the integer 1 keep their meaning. For example, defines preferred-plus serialization (its Section 4) and deterministic serialization (its Section 5), and its deterministic serialization excludes NaNs other than 0xf97e00. Once published as an RFC, its deterministic serialization could be identified by the URL of the section of that RFC that defines it, with the fragment. Its preferred-plus serialization is not deterministic when the value contains a map (its Section 5.3.2), so it is not an encoding for this parameter.

Other encodings, of CBOR or of other content such as JSON, are identified by URLs that the application profiles that use them name (); this document does not list them. A URL is not the integer 1, even when it links to Section 4.2.1 of : a verifier compares a URL only with the URLs of the encodings it implements.

section.name: Producers
section.t: When a producer creates the preimage by applying a deterministic encoding to a structured value, it SHOULD include deterministic-encodings, so that a verifier holding only the structured value can re-create the preimage. When present, the value MUST identify the encoding actually applied. A producer that serializes a structured value without a deterministic encoding, or whose preimage is not the serialization of a structured value -- for example application/octet-stream content, an image, or an archive -- has no encoding to identify, and the parameter is absent; the content binding can then be checked only from the preimage bytes.

section.name: Consistency with preimage-content-type
section.t: The Applicable Content Types of the encoding that the integer 1 identifies () are application/cbor, application/cbor-seq, application/cose, application/cose-key, application/cose-key-set, application/cose-x509, application/cwt, and application/multipart-core, and media types with the +cbor, +cbor-seq, +cose, +cwt, or +sd-cwt structured syntax suffix. When deterministic-encodings is present, preimage-content-type (259) MUST also be present, and its value MUST match one of the Applicable Content Types of the encoding that deterministic-encodings identifies:

li.t: A 259 value that is a media-type name matches when its type and subtype -- with any parameters removed, and compared case-insensitively ( Section 4.2) -- equal a listed media type, or when its subtype ends in a listed structured syntax suffix ( Section 4.2.8).
A 259 value that is a Content-Format number matches when the CoAP Content-Formats registry ( Section 12.3) assigns that number to a matching media type with no content coding.

section.t: A producer MUST NOT emit a Hash Envelope that violates these rules -- for example, one pairing the integer 1 with application/json. A verifier that implements the encoding that deterministic-encodings identifies, and finds preimage-content-type (259) absent or with a value that does not match the Applicable Content Types of that encoding, MUST treat the check of the content binding as failed, without attempting recomputation. This check comes first, and takes precedence over . A verifier that does not implement the identified encoding, like one that implements only , ignores the parameter, and its results are unchanged.

section.name: Verifying the Content Binding
section.t: A verifier that holds the preimage itself -- for example, as retrieved from payload-location (260) -- checks the content binding as Section 5.3 describes: it checks whether the digest of the preimage, produced with the hash algorithm identified by payload-hash-alg (258), matches the payload. That check needs no encoding information, and applies whether or not deterministic-encodings is present, subject to .

A verifier that holds only a structured value -- for example, content it received, stored, or decoded in a form other than the preimage itself -- has to re-create the preimage by encoding that value. When deterministic-encodings identifies an encoding the verifier implements, the verifier MUST encode the value with that encoding, and MUST NOT infer the encoding from preimage-content-type (259) or from the structure of the value. If the digest of the result does not match the payload, the check fails. It also fails if the verifier cannot produce that encoding of the value -- for example, when the value holds a NaN with a payload that its encoder does not support ().

When deterministic-encodings is absent, or its value does not identify an encoding the verifier implements -- for example, a URL that the verifier's application profile does not name, an integer other than 1, or a value of another type, such as the floating-point number 1.0 -- the verifier ignores the parameter, and checks the content binding as it would for a Hash Envelope without it, as Section 5.3 describes. A verifier that holds no preimage then has nothing to hash, and the check fails. This document adds no other outcome.

A Hash Envelope produced without this parameter -- including any produced before the parameter was registered -- is not defective: its content binding can still be verified from the preimage bytes. Signature validity is unaffected by the check of the content binding: a verifier that has not established the content binding can still validate the signature of the COSE_Sign1 as specified in .

section.name: Examples
section.t: These use Extended Diagnostic Notation ( Appendix G), in the style of Section 4.1; signature and key material are truncated.

The structured value {"b": 2, "a": 1}, a CBOR map, encoded per the Core Deterministic Encoding Requirements of Section 4.2.1 (bytewise key order, placing "a" before "b"), gives the 7-octet preimage a2616101616202, whose SHA-256 digest is a0d3af9e86e5517f729bad0657e2c6f3b7d03899894c8d6b33759074c893b5e3:
section.artwork: 18([ # COSE_Sign1 <<{ / alg / 1: -7, # ES256 / hash algorithm / 258: -16, # sha-256 / preimage type / 259: "application/cbor", / deterministic encodings / TBD_1: 1, # RFC 8949, Section 4.2.1 }>> / unprotected / {}, / payload / h'a0d3af9e...c893b5e3', # digest above / signature / h'...' # 64 octets, r || s ])
section.t: registers application/swid+cbor for Concise Software Identification (CoSWID) tags but does not require a deterministic encoding of them, so two producers may serialize the same tag as different byte sequences. A producer that applies the Core Deterministic Encoding Requirements before hashing a CoSWID tag sets preimage-content-type (259) to application/swid+cbor and deterministic-encodings to the integer 1 () -- recording its own choice, not a CoSWID requirement -- so that a verifier holding the decoded tag knows how to re-create the preimage.

A Hash Envelope over JSON content can carry deterministic-encodings with the URL of a specification that defines a deterministic encoding of JSON, such as "https://json-spec.example/deterministic", with preimage-content-type "application/json", when the application profile the producer follows names that URL. This document does not name it. A verifier that implements that encoding and holds the decoded JSON value re-creates the preimage with it. A verifier that does not implement it ignores the parameter, and checks the content binding as Section 5.3 describes ().

section.name: Security Considerations
section.t: A deterministic encoding fixes the preimage for a given structured value, so decoding a preimage and encoding the result again reproduces the preimage only if decoding preserved that value exactly. Decoding into a programming language's native types can lose distinctions the encoding depends on -- for example, between integer and floating-point numbers, or the presence of a tag. Choices that decide which data item represents a value, such as those Section 4.2.2 leaves to each protocol for tags and for integer versus floating-point values, belong to the structured value, not to the encoding that deterministic-encodings identifies. A choice that changes only how the same data item is serialized, such as encoding every floating-point value as binary64, is a different encoding, not the one that the integer 1 identifies (). A producer that re-reads stored content before hashing MUST ensure the preimage it hashes is byte-identical to the encoding's own output. A verifier that re-creates a preimage from a structured value () needs that value exactly as the producer encoded it; otherwise its recomputed digest can differ from the payload, and the check of the content binding then fails.

A verifier does not dereference a URL in deterministic-encodings, so the value causes no network access, and a URL whose resource has moved or changed does not change the verifier's result. A value that does not identify an encoding the verifier implements has no effect on the result ().

section.name: Privacy Considerations
section.t: A digest over deterministically encoded content is a stable function of that content, so the payload is linkable wherever the content recurs. If the structured value comes from a low-entropy space, encoding and hashing candidate values can recover it; this risk already exists wherever is used, and identifying the encoding removes an ambiguity that might have slowed such an attempt.

section.name: COSE Header Parameters
section.t: IANA is requested to register the following entry in the "COSE Header Parameters" registry, in the "Integer values from 256 to 65535" range, under the Specification Required policy ( Section 4.6) that governs that range:

tr.td: Deterministic encoding applied to create the preimage of a Hash Envelope payload

section.t: The suggested value for TBD_1 is 271, the lowest unassigned value in the "Integer values from 256 to 65535" range of the COSE Header Parameters registry as of 2026-11-23.

front.title: Key words for use in RFCs to Indicate Requirement Levels

abstract.t: In many standards track documents several words are used to signify the requirements in the specification. These words are often capitalized. This document defines these words as they should be interpreted in IETF documents. This document specifies an Internet Best Current Practices for the Internet Community, and requests discussion and suggestions for improvements.

front.title: Ambiguity of Uppercase vs Lowercase in RFC 2119 Key Words

abstract.t: RFC 2119 specifies common key words that may be used in protocol specifications. This document aims to reduce the ambiguity by clarifying that only UPPERCASE usage of the key words have the defined special meanings.

front.title: Media Type Specifications and Registration Procedures

abstract.t: This document defines procedures for the specification and registration of media types for use in HTTP, MIME, and other Internet protocols. This memo documents an Internet Best Current Practice.

The Constrained Application Protocol (CoAP) is a specialized web transfer protocol for use with constrained nodes and constrained (e.g., low-power, lossy) networks. The nodes often have 8-bit microcontrollers with small amounts of ROM and RAM, while constrained networks such as IPv6 over Low-Power Wireless Personal Area Networks (6LoWPANs) often have high packet error rates and a typical throughput of 10s of kbit/s. The protocol is designed for machine- to-machine (M2M) applications such as smart energy and building automation.

CoAP provides a request/response interaction model between application endpoints, supports built-in discovery of services and resources, and includes key concepts of the Web such as URIs and Internet media types. CoAP is designed to easily interface with HTTP for integration with the Web while meeting specialized requirements such as multicast support, very low overhead, and simplicity for constrained environments.

front.title: Guidelines for Writing an IANA Considerations Section in RFCs

abstract.t: Many protocols make use of points of extensibility that use constants to identify various protocol parameters. To ensure that the values in these fields do not have conflicting uses and to promote interoperability, their allocations are often coordinated by a central record keeper. For IETF protocols, that role is filled by the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA).

To make assignments in a given registry prudently, guidance describing the conditions under which new values should be assigned, as well as when and how modifications to existing values can be made, is needed. This document defines a framework for the documentation of these guidelines by specification authors, in order to assure that the provided guidance for the IANA Considerations is clear and addresses the various issues that are likely in the operation of a registry.
This is the third edition of this document; it obsoletes RFC 5226.

front.title: Concise Data Definition Language (CDDL): A Notational Convention to Express Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR) and JSON Data Structures

abstract.t: This document proposes a notational convention to express Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR) data structures (RFC 7049). Its main goal is to provide an easy and unambiguous way to express structures for protocol messages and data formats that use CBOR or JSON.

This document describes the Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR) Sequence format and associated media type "application/cbor-seq". A CBOR Sequence consists of any number of encoded CBOR data items, simply concatenated in sequence.

Structured syntax suffixes for media types allow other media types to build on them and make it explicit that they are built on an existing media type as their foundation. This specification defines and registers "+cbor-seq" as a structured syntax suffix for CBOR Sequences.

A Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) is a compact sequence of characters that identifies an abstract or physical resource. This specification defines the generic URI syntax and a process for resolving URI references that might be in relative form, along with guidelines and security considerations for the use of URIs on the Internet. The URI syntax defines a grammar that is a superset of all valid URIs, allowing an implementation to parse the common components of a URI reference without knowing the scheme-specific requirements of every possible identifier. This specification does not define a generative grammar for URIs; that task is performed by the individual specifications of each URI scheme. [STANDARDS-TRACK]

The Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) is a stateless application-level protocol for distributed, collaborative, hypertext information systems. This document describes the overall architecture of HTTP, establishes common terminology, and defines aspects of the protocol that are shared by all versions. In this definition are core protocol elements, extensibility mechanisms, and the "http" and "https" Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) schemes.
This document updates RFC 3864 and obsoletes RFCs 2818, 7231, 7232, 7233, 7235, 7538, 7615, 7694, and portions of 7230.

The Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR) is a data format whose design goals include the possibility of extremely small code size, fairly small message size, and extensibility without the need for version negotiation. These design goals make it different from earlier binary serializations such as ASN.1 and MessagePack.

This document obsoletes RFC 7049, providing editorial improvements, new details, and errata fixes while keeping full compatibility with the interchange format of RFC 7049. It does not create a new version of the format.

front.title: CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE): Structures and Process

abstract.t: Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR) is a data format designed for small code size and small message size. There is a need to be able to define basic security services for this data format. This document defines the CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE) protocol. This specification describes how to create and process signatures, message authentication codes, and encryption using CBOR for serialization. This specification additionally describes how to represent cryptographic keys using CBOR.
This document, along with RFC 9053, obsoletes RFC 8152.

front.title: CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE) Hash Envelope

abstract.t: This document defines new CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE) header parameters for signaling a payload as an output of a hash function. This mechanism enables faster validation, as access to the original payload is not required for signature validation. Additionally, hints of the hashed payload's content format and availability are defined, providing references to optional discovery mechanisms that can help to find the original payload content.

RFC 8949 defines CBOR, a standard for serializing data types such as integers, strings, and arrays into encoded bytes. CBOR serialization is flexible, allowing data types to be encoded in multiple ways to accommodate deployment in constrained environments.
This document introduces the term “general serialization” for the full set of encodings permitted by RFC 8949, and formally defines two specific serializations: preferred-plus serialization, which differs from preferred serialization only in cases rarely encountered in practice and is recommended for broad use; and deterministic serialization, which likewise differs only in rarely encountered cases from core deterministic encoding defined in RFC 8949.
This document updates RFC 8949 with a new rule that limits how new tag definitions can affect the CBOR data model.
This document provides clarifications to RFC 8949 regarding bignums and floating-point NaN handling, along with general background information on serialization, determinism, and CBOR byte-string wrapping.

front.title: (Extensible Markup Language) XML-Signature Syntax and Processing

abstract.t: This document specifies XML (Extensible Markup Language) digital signature processing rules and syntax. [STANDARDS-TRACK]

ISO/IEC 19770-2:2015 Software Identification (SWID) tags provide an extensible XML-based structure to identify and describe individual software components, patches, and installation bundles. SWID tag representations can be too large for devices with network and storage constraints. This document defines a concise representation of SWID tags: Concise SWID (CoSWID) tags. CoSWID supports a set of semantics and features that are similar to those for SWID tags, as well as new semantics that allow CoSWIDs to describe additional types of information, all in a more memory-efficient format.

An Entity Attestation Token (EAT) provides an attested claims set that describes the state and characteristics of an entity, a device such as a smartphone, an Internet of Things (IoT) device, network equipment, or such. This claims set is used by a relying party, server, or service to determine the type and degree of trust placed in the entity.
An EAT is either a CBOR Web Token (CWT) or a JSON Web Token (JWT) with attestation-oriented claims.

li.t: The value of deterministic-encodings is the integer 1 or a URL (). The integer 1 identifies the Core Deterministic Encoding Requirements of Section 4.2.1, which version 02 identified by the URL of that section; the integer takes 1 byte, the URL 59. Any other encoding is still identified by a URL that an application profile names. This document creates no registry and defines no other integer value.

A producer that applied the Core Deterministic Encoding Requirements sets the parameter to the integer 1, not to a URL (). A verifier of this version ignores the URL that version 02 listed (, ). Version 00 used the integer 1 for the same encoding, through a registry that version 01 removed.
A verifier also ignores an integer other than 1 and a value of another type, such as the floating-point number 1.0 (). The example in carries the integer 1.
Editorial: the fragment rule cites Section 4.2.5; the text no longer predicts a section number of once it is an RFC; the eat_profile precedent names a profile by a URI or an OID ().

The value of deterministic-encodings became a URL, not a token: an "https" URL that links to the section of a specification that defines the encoding (). Version 01 used the text string "dtrm", the name gives to deterministic serialization in its CDDL control operator. A URL needs no registry: the application profile that names a URL is responsible for it.

Version 02 listed one URL, for CBOR content: the URL of Section 4.2.1 of , the Core Deterministic Encoding Requirements, with its fragment. A URL for a document that defines more than one encoding, such as or , carries a section fragment (). An RFC does not change, so the URL needs no replacement later. Unlike "dtrm", this encoding does not exclude NaNs other than 0xf97e00: the representation of NaN values is one of the choices that Section 4.2.2 leaves to a protocol.

Other URLs are named by the application profiles that use the parameter, not by this document (, ). A verifier ignores a URL it does not implement, so an arbitrary URL changes no verification outcome.

The outcome "unverified" is removed: the check of a content binding succeeds or fails, as Section 5.3 describes it. A verifier of version 02 ignored deterministic-encodings when it was absent or its value was not the URL of an encoding the verifier implemented, including the text string "dtrm", and checked the content binding as for a Hash Envelope without it. When a verifier cannot produce the identified encoding of a structured value, the check fails. Only a verifier that implements the identified encoding checks preimage-content-type (259) against it (, ).
Examples showed the URL and a JSON case with a URL that this document does not list (); Security Considerations state that the URL is not dereferenced ().

The abstract and the introduction no longer rest on RFC 8949 describing more than one deterministic encoding. The introduction shows instead a value that has two valid CBOR encodings, one of them deterministic, and why stating the encoding lets a verifier tell a modified value from one encoded another way ().
The "COSE Deterministic Encodings" registry is removed. This document requests only the registration of the header parameter ().

The value of deterministic-encodings became the text string "dtrm", the name gives to its deterministic serialization. Version 00 used the integer 1, the value its registry assigned to core-deterministic. A verifier of version 01 handled the integer 1 as a value it did not recognize.
"dtrm" excludes non-trivial NaNs, as defines. In version 00, value 1 was Section 4.2.1 without that exclusion.
The Applicable Content Types, which version 00 put in the registry entry, are listed in .
In version 01, a verifier that could not produce the identified encoding of a structured value reported the content binding as unverified.
